FACT: Compositional Kernel Synthesis with a Three-Stage Agentic Workflow

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: ; ; ISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/26/09CCS: Computing methodologies Parallel computing methodologiesCCS: Computing methodologies Machine learningCCS: Software and its engineering
Sina Heidari email: sinaheidari@vt.edu Affiliation: Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA and Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos email: dsn@vt.edu Affiliation: Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia, USA
2026
Abstract.

Deep learning compilers and vendor libraries deliver strong baseline performance but are bounded by finite, engineer-curated catalogs. When these omit needed optimizations, practitioners substitute hand-written CUDA or CUTLASS, demanding expertise in GPU microarchitecture and C++ template metaprogramming. Recent LLM-based agents target kernel generation in raw CUDA, forcing rediscovery of optimizations already encoded in mature libraries.

We present FACT (Framework for Agentic CUTLASS Transpilation), a framework that employs a three-stage, agent-driven workflow optimizing PyTorch modules through multi-pattern composition while grounding synthesis in CUTLASS C++. (1) Pattern discovery: an LLM agent inspects the traced graph, matches subgraphs to optimization rules, retrieves vetted examples from an architecture-specific index, and outputs prioritized patterns. (2) Pattern realization: each pattern is implemented as a CUTLASS kernel wrapped in a PyTorch extension, verified, and auto-tuned by sweeping parameters inferred from the CUTLASS hierarchy. (3) Pattern composition: extensions are loaded together into a single composed module for end-to-end benchmarking.

We evaluate the workflow using KernelBench’s evaluation framework and provided modules on an NVIDIA A100. On Level 1, we apply the workflow to three GEMM workloads (square matrix multiply, batched matrix multiply, and large-KK matrix multiply). Auto-tuned CUTLASS kernels improve over PyTorch cuBLAS baseline by 1.06×1.06\times–1.18×1.18\times. On Level 3 MiniGPT block, composing fused multi-head attention with fused MLP GEMM+GELU yields 2.79×2.79\times end-to-end speedup. Our work couples agentic graph-level pattern discovery with auto-tuning and a dynamic pattern table, offering a practical path from traced PyTorch to deployable kernels by automating CUTLASS kernel synthesis and auto-tuning.

Keywords: 
CUTLASS Kernel Synthesis, Architecture-aware Optimization, Agentic Code Generation, GPU Kernel Optimization, Multi-pattern Composition, Large Language Models

1. Introduction

Deep learning compilers such as TVM (Chen et al., 2018), Ansor (Zheng et al., 2020), and PyTorch Inductor (Ansel et al., 2024) have made significant strides in automating the compilation of tensor programs. However, their ability to generate high-performance GPU kernels is fundamentally constrained by the optimization patterns that their developers have codified. When a new model architecture or a new GPU generation is released, developing optimized kernels that exploit its novel hardware features requires significant engineering effort, and integrating these optimizations into compiler backends adds further delay before they become available to practitioners. Even when optimized kernels are eventually integrated into a compiler—as CUrator (Lee et al., 2025) does by incorporating CUTLASS (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025) into TVM’s Bring-Your-Own-Codegen (BYOC) pipeline—the compiler relies on a fixed, developer-specified pattern registry for graph node matching and fusion, which cannot discover or add new optimization patterns without manual intervention.

The alternative to waiting for compiler support is to hand-optimize kernels using low-level languages such as CUDA or vendor-specific template libraries such as CUTLASS. Expert GPU programmers can write custom kernels that exploit architecture-specific features and integrate them into a PyTorch computation graph via custom extensions. This approach routinely achieves performance competitive with or exceeding compiler output, but it demands deep expertise in GPU microarchitecture and months of engineering effort per kernel.

Over the past two years, large language model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in code generation, program synthesis, and multi-step reasoning (Ouyang et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). These capabilities have been applied directly to GPU kernel optimization: CUDA Agent (Dai et al., 2026) scales agentic reinforcement learning to generate high-performance CUDA kernels; KernelBlaster (Dong et al., 2026) uses memory-augmented in-context RL to transfer optimization knowledge across tasks; Astra (Wei et al., 2025) employs a multi-agent workflow to iteratively transform existing kernels using profiling-driven feedback; and StitchCUDA (Li et al., 2026) targets end-to-end GPU programs with a planner/coder/verifier decomposition.

However, these approaches share a common limitation: they synthesize kernels in raw CUDA, which forces them to rediscover—in generated source code—optimizations that mature libraries have already encapsulated as vetted, architecture-parameterized templates. Despite the promise of agentic kernel optimization, we are not aware of any prior framework that combines library-grounded synthesis with a dynamic pattern registry—addressing both the static registry limitation of compiler-based approaches and the raw-code generation focus of prior agentic systems.

We propose FACT, a framework that combines multi-pattern composition with library-grounded synthesis through a dynamic pattern registry that grows as the agent discovers new patterns—where each pattern corresponds to a subgraph identifiable by an optimization rule (e.g., GEMM, FMHA), data type, and target GPU architecture—unlike static registries, this enables accumulation across workloads. FACT performs architecture-specific synthesis by matching patterns to the target GPU’s capabilities. It also enables architecture-specific auto-tuning where the agent automatically infers which parameters to sweep at each level of CUTLASS’s hierarchical API.

FACT realizes this through a three-stage agentic workflow. (1) Pattern Discovery: an LLM agent analyzes the PyTorch computation graph and proposes optimization patterns by retrieving vetted examples from an architecture-specific kernel repository. (2) Pattern Realization: each pattern is implemented as a CUTLASS kernel, verified for correctness, auto-tuned, and added to the dynamic pattern registry. (3) Pattern Composition: realized kernels are composed with the original computation graph for end-to-end benchmarking.

Both synthesis and auto-tuning navigate CUTLASS’s three-level hierarchy. At the tile level, synthesis configures Tensor Core primitives. At the kernel level, synthesis selects pipelining strategies appropriate for the target architecture. At the grid level, synthesis chooses scheduling policies that balance load across thread blocks. These levels must be addressed coherently—incompatible choices across levels cause failures. Auto-tuning sweeps parameters at each level (tile shapes, pipeline stages, split-K factors) to find optimal configurations. The architecture-specific kernel repository grounds both processes in vetted instantiations.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    Library-grounded agentic kernel synthesis with a dynamic pattern registry. We ground the agent’s synthesis in CUTLASS C++ templates rather than raw CUDA, enabling reuse of architecture-parameterized patterns that accumulate across workloads.

  • •

    Architecture-specific auto-tuning where the agent infers relevant parameters based on the target architecture and kernel type. For Ampere multistage pipelines, the agent sweeps tile shapes and pipeline stages; for Hopper warp-specialized kernels, it sweeps kernel schedules and cluster shapes. The search space is derived from CUTLASS’s architecture-specific instantiations.

  • •

    KernelBench-style evaluation on representative problems spanning CUTLASS’s capabilities. We demonstrate the workflow on GEMM variants exercising different scheduling policies (Data-Parallel, Batched, Stream-K) and on a multi-pattern transformer block, achieving speedups of 1.06×\times–2.79×\times.

2. Background & Motivation

2.1. KernelBench Evaluation Framework

KernelBench (Ouyang et al., 2025) introduces a standardized benchmark for evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on the task of generating optimized GPU kernels. The framework adopts a two-stage evaluation methodology centered on correctness verification and performance measurement. In the correctness stage, kernels synthesized by the agent are compiled and executed against a reference PyTorch implementation; the output tensors are compared element-wise to ensure functional equivalence. This stage verifies that the agent-generated kernel preserves the semantics of the original computation graph. In the performance stage, correctly executing kernels are benchmarked using CUDA events to measure end-to-end execution time on target GPU hardware. KernelBench reports speedup relative to a baseline—typically the standard PyTorch eager-mode execution or a vendor library implementation—thereby quantifying the optimization capability of the agent.

A key contribution of KernelBench is its hierarchical task formulation across three difficulty tiers. Level 1 tasks involve single linear algebra operators (e.g., matrix multiplication, transpose) that directly map to established library patterns. Level 2 tasks introduce fused operators that combine two or more primitive operations, requiring the agent to discover and implement kernel fusion optimizations. Level 3 tasks present complex computation blocks from real deep learning models, challenging the agent to navigate multi-operator patterns and interdependent scheduling decisions. This progressive difficulty structure enables granular assessment of agent capabilities across different levels of optimization complexity.

Crucially, KernelBench defines the optimization problem as transpiling a baseline PyTorch module into a functionally equivalent kernel implementation. The input to the agent is a PyTorch computation graph extracted from the target model. The agent’s objective is to synthesize optimized code that, when compiled and loaded as a PyTorch extension, replaces the baseline subgraph in the model’s execution trace. This formulation closely mirrors real-world workflows in which practitioners identify performance-critical subgraphs through profiling and replace them with custom kernels. By standardizing both the input format (computation graphs) and the evaluation protocol (correctness checking followed by performance benchmarking), KernelBench provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing kernel generation agents across diverse hardware architectures and operator patterns.

3. Task Definition

We adopt a task formulation aligned with KernelBench’s transpilation paradigm, with two key extensions. First, we target multi-pattern composition rather than isolated operator synthesis: the agent operates over the complete computation graph of a baseline PyTorch model and produces a transformed version that reflects kernel-level optimizations applied at multiple subgraphs. Second, we introduce a dynamic pattern table that serves as a persistent optimization catalog, enabling discovered patterns to be reused across models and accumulated over time.

Formally, let 𝒢=(V,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,E) denote the computation graph of a baseline PyTorch model, where each node v∈Vv\in V represents a tensor operation and each edge e∈Ee\in E represents a data dependency. The agent’s objective is to discover a set of optimization opportunities 𝒫={p1,p2,…,pn}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n}\}, where each pattern pip_{i} corresponds to a subgraph 𝒢i⊆𝒢\mathcal{G}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{G} that can be replaced by an optimized kernel implementation. Each pattern pip_{i} is associated with a rule—such as GEMM, FMHA (Fused Multi-Head Attention), or epilogue fusion—that determines the structural template of the kernel synthesis problem.

The pattern table 𝒯\mathcal{T} serves as the central abstraction for organizing and retrieving kernel implementations. Each entry in 𝒯\mathcal{T} maps a tuple (r,τ,α)(r,\tau,\alpha) to a concrete CUTLASS kernel implementation, where rr denotes the optimization rule, τ\tau denotes the data type configuration (e.g., FP32, BF16, FP8), and α\alpha denotes the target GPU architecture (e.g., Ampere, Hopper). This multi-dimensional indexing enables the agent to select kernel instantiations that match the computational pattern, data type constraints, and hardware context. Importantly, the table is dynamic: when the agent discovers a new pattern and synthesizes a correct kernel implementation, the pattern and its associated kernel are added to 𝒯\mathcal{T}, expanding the optimization catalog for future queries.

Figure 1 illustrates the pattern mapping hierarchy. At the top level, the agent identifies patterns from the computation graph, each corresponding to a well-defined optimization rule. For each rule, the pattern table maintains multiple CUTLASS kernel implementations specialized across data types, input shapes, and GPU architectures. This design enables efficient retrieval: given a target subgraph, data type constraints, and hardware platform, the agent can query 𝒯\mathcal{T} to retrieve candidate kernels, then benchmark them to select the highest-performing variant. Unlike static pattern libraries in which all possible specializations must be known ahead of time, our dynamic table allows the optimization catalog to grow as the agent encounters new patterns and architectures.

4. Proposed Approach

Figure 2 illustrates our three-stage agentic workflow for whole-model kernel optimization. The workflow maps directly to CUTLASS’s API hierarchy (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025) and leverages LLM-based actions to orchestrate complex optimization tasks that would otherwise require manual intervention. Each stage decomposes into a sequence of well-defined actions—graph extraction and analysis, kernel synthesis and verification, composition and extension loading—that the agent executes systematically. By structuring optimization as a pipeline of discrete actions, we enable the agent to reason about each decision point independently while maintaining coherence across the entire workflow.

4.1. Pattern Discovery

The first stage begins with the baseline PyTorch model and executes five sequential actions to discover optimization opportunities.

Action 1: Read instruction template. The agent first reads an instruction template that defines the pattern discovery task. This template specifies the optimization objectives, the target GPU architecture, data type constraints, and examples of CUTLASS patterns to search for. The instruction grounds the agent’s analysis in domain knowledge about CUTLASS capabilities.

Action 2: Analyze computation graph. Using PyTorch’s tracing mechanism, the agent extracts the computation graph 𝒢=(V,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,E) as a sequence of tensor operations. This analysis preserves operator semantics, tensor shapes, and data type information. The agent then performs structural pattern matching to locate subgraphs that correspond to known CUTLASS patterns: linear algebra operations (GEMM, GEMV), attention mechanisms (FMHA), convolutional layers (Conv2D), and epilogue fusion opportunities (activation functions, bias operations). During this analysis, the agent may not find exact matches in the examples index; however, it can retrieve multiple examples that, when combined, provide the necessary components to realize the target pattern.

Action 3: Query examples index. For each candidate subgraph, the agent queries an examples index to retrieve relevant CUTLASS kernel implementations. This index contains architecture-specific examples organized by optimization rule, data type, and input shape. By retrieving similar examples, the agent grounds its pattern proposals in proven implementations rather than synthesizing kernels from scratch.

Table 1 summarizes the available CUTLASS examples across KernelBench difficulty levels and GPU architectures. Level 1 tasks involve single linear algebra operators (e.g., basic GEMM, convolution) that directly map to established library patterns. Level 2 tasks introduce fused operators that combine two or more primitive operations (e.g., GEMM with epilogue fusion such as bias, ReLU, softmax; gather/scatter fusion). Level 3 tasks present complex computation blocks from real deep learning models (e.g., fused multi-head attention, grouped operations, multi-GEMM fusion), challenging the agent to navigate multi-operator patterns and interdependent scheduling decisions.

Action 4: Propose patterns. Based on the subgraph analysis and retrieved examples, the agent proposes a set of optimization patterns 𝒫proposed={p1,p2,…,pm}\mathcal{P}_{\text{proposed}}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{m}\}. Each proposed pattern includes the subgraph to be optimized, the associated optimization rule (e.g., GEMM, FMHA), and references to the retrieved examples that guide kernel synthesis.

Action 5: Prioritize patterns. The agent prioritizes the proposed patterns based on expected performance impact and implementation complexity. This prioritization considers factors such as operator granularity, memory access patterns, and the quality of retrieved examples. The output is an ordered list of prioritized patterns 𝒫={p1,p2,…,pn}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n}\} that are passed to the next stage for kernel synthesis.

4.2. Pattern Realization

The second stage synthesizes concrete CUTLASS kernels for each prioritized pattern. For each pattern pi∈𝒫p_{i}\in\mathcal{P}, the agent executes an iterative workflow with six actions, including a feedback loop for correctness verification and an optional auto-tuning step.

Action 1: Select supporting examples. The agent queries the examples index to retrieve CUTLASS kernel implementations that serve as references for synthesizing the target pattern. These supporting examples are selected based on similarity to the target pattern in terms of optimization rule, data type, input shape, and GPU architecture. The agent may retrieve multiple examples that, when combined, provide the necessary components to realize the pattern.

Action 2: Synthesize CUTLASS + PyTorch extension. Guided by the supporting examples, the agent synthesizes a CUTLASS kernel implementation. This synthesis operates at CUTLASS’s three API levels (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025), organized from innermost to outermost as shown in Figure 3.

At the tile level (innermost circle), the agent configures matrix multiply primitives for Tensor Core efficiency. This involves selecting the appropriate instruction shape, operand datatypes, swizzling mode, and memory layout (MN-major vs K-major).

At the kernel level (middle circle), the agent selects a software pipelining strategy appropriate for the target architecture. For Hopper GPUs, warp-specialized designs dedicate producer warps to TMA loads and consumer warps to WGMMA compute, leveraging warpgroup register reallocation. For Ampere GPUs, multistage pipelines use cp.async to prefetch data while computing on the current buffer, with all warps taking dual roles.

At the grid level (outermost circle), the agent configures work partitioning across thread blocks to ensure load balance and high device utilization. CUTLASS supports Data Parallel (standard 2D tiling), Split-K (partitioning along K dimension with turnstile reduction), and Stream-K (persistent CTAs processing fractional tiles to eliminate wave quantization).

The synthesized kernel is wrapped as a PyTorch extension, compiled into a shared library (.so file), and registered as a custom operation.

Action 3: Create per-pattern ModelNew(nn.Module). The agent constructs a new PyTorch module, ModelNew, that integrates the synthesized CUTLASS extension. This module inherits from nn.Module and implements the forward method to invoke the custom CUTLASS operation. The module preserves the input/output interface of the original subgraph, enabling drop-in replacement within the computation graph.

Action 4: Verification and benchmarking. The agent executes ModelNew against a reference implementation using identical test inputs. For correctness verification, output tensors are compared element-wise to ensure functional equivalence. For performance benchmarking, the kernel is executed multiple times on the target GPU hardware, and CUDA events measure end-to-end execution time. The resulting speedup relative to the baseline PyTorch implementation is recorded.

At this point, the agent evaluates whether the pattern is accepted. If the pattern passes both correctness verification and achieves satisfactory performance, the workflow proceeds to Action 5. If the pattern fails verification or performs poorly, the workflow loops back to Action 1: the agent re-selects supporting examples, inspects the synthesized code to identify correctness issues, and modifies the implementation to fix the problems. This iterative refinement continues until the pattern is accepted.

Action 5: Auto-tune kernel. After a pattern passes correctness verification, the agent may perform auto-tuning to improve performance beyond the initial configuration. The auto-tuning search space is not hardcoded—it is inferred from the three CUTLASS API levels chosen during Action 2. At the tile level, the agent reads the CUTLASS test files for the target architecture and data type to extract all valid threadblock and warp tile shapes used in existing instantiations, forming the set of tile candidates to sweep. At the kernel level, the swept parameter depends on the pipelining strategy: for Ampere multistage pipelines the agent sweeps the number of pipeline stages (typically 2–3, constrained by shared-memory capacity), whereas for Hopper warp-specialized kernels the pipeline depth is managed automatically by TMA and the agent instead sweeps the kernel schedule (e.g., KernelTmaWarpSpecialized vs. KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong) and cluster shapes. At the grid level, Split-K problems sweep the split-K factor, while Data Parallel and Stream-K schedules require no additional parameter.

To avoid recompiling a separate binary for each configuration, the agent uses a parameterized code generator that emits a single .cu file containing multiple template instantiations—one per variant—compiled into one shared library with a runtime dispatch index. An auto-tuning script sweeps the full search space, benchmarks each configuration (warmup + timed iterations with CUDA synchronization), records GFLOPS and hardware efficiency, and saves the complete results as JSON. The best-performing configuration is selected and used in subsequent stages.

Action 6: Add to pattern table. Once a pattern is accepted, the agent adds it to the dynamic pattern table 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The entry includes the pattern pip_{i}, the synthesized CUTLASS kernel implementation, the auto-tuning results (if performed), the benchmark results (speedup metrics), and metadata about the supporting examples used. The entry is indexed by the tuple (r,τ,α)(r,\tau,\alpha), enabling future queries to retrieve the kernel without re-synthesis. This action expands the optimization catalog, allowing the agent to accumulate knowledge across patterns and reuse kernels for similar workloads.

4.3. Pattern Composition

The third stage assembles the realized kernels into an optimized model ready for deployment. The composition action constructs a new computation graph 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime} by replacing each subgraph 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} with a placeholder node that invokes the corresponding CUTLASS kernel. This transformation preserves the semantic equivalence of the model while replacing suboptimal PyTorch operators with specialized kernels.

The agent then executes an extension loading action. Each kernel is compiled into a shared library (.so file) and registered as a PyTorch custom op. The compiled extensions are loaded into the Python runtime, making the optimized kernels callable from PyTorch’s eager execution mode and torchscript compilation path.

With the extensions loaded, the agent performs end-to-end benchmarking of the optimized model. The baseline model and the optimized model are executed on identical inputs, and wall-clock time measures the overall speedup. This action validates that the composition of individual kernel optimizations translates to model-level performance improvement.

The final output is an optimized PyTorch model with CUTLASS kernels integrated as extensions, ready for deployment in inference or training workloads. The dynamic pattern table 𝒯\mathcal{T} persists across optimization sessions, enabling the agent to accumulate optimization knowledge and reuse kernels across different models and architectures.

5. Performance Evaluation

5.1. Experimental Setup

Hardware. All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU (Ampere architecture, SM80), which provides a theoretical peak throughput of 156 TFLOPS in TF32 tensor core mode (NVIDIA Corporation, 2020). Additional patterns targeting the H200 GPU (Hopper architecture, SM90) are under development and will be reported in future work.

Benchmark problems. We evaluate on three KernelBench Level 1 problems drawn from the GEMM family (Problems 1, 3, and 6), each exercising a different grid-level scheduling policy, and on KernelBench Level 3 problem 44_MiniGPTBlock, a MiniGPT-style transformer block with batch size 128, sequence length 512, and embedding width 768. Problem 1 computes C=A×BC=A\times B for 4096×40964096\times 4096 matrices in FP32, exercising a standard square GEMM workload that maps directly to CUTLASS’s TF32 tensor-op GEMM template with Data Parallel scheduling. Problem 3 computes a batched matrix multiplication C⁡[b]=A⁡[b]×B⁡[b]C[b]=A[b]\times B[b] for b∈[0,128)b\in[0,128) with per-batch dimensions 512×1024512\times 1024 and 1024×20481024\times 2048, evaluating Batched GEMM via CUTLASS’s kBatched mode. Problem 6 computes C=A×BC=A\times B for 256×524,288256\times 524{,}288 and 524,288×256524{,}288\times 256 matrices, stressing the K dimension to evaluate Stream-K grid-level scheduling. Together, Problems 1, 3, and 6 span the three dominant scheduling regimes for GEMM on modern GPUs; Problem 44_MiniGPTBlock exercises multi-pattern realization and Stage 3 composition.

Software environment. Kernels were implemented using CUTLASS 3.8.0 (git commit ea46e277), compiled with NVCC 12.4.131 through PyTorch’s torch.utils.cpp_extension interface, and loaded as custom CUDA extensions. All experiments were conducted on Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 6.17.0-14-generic, x86_64) with CUDA 12.4 and PyTorch 2.4.1+cu124. Random inputs were generated using torch.manual.seed(42) for reproducibility. The baseline for all comparisons is PyTorch 2.4.1 eager-mode execution with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True, which dispatches torch.matmul and torch.bmm to cuBLAS’s TF32 tensor core GEMM implementation. For compiler baseline comparisons, we additionally evaluated PyTorch Inductor (using torch.compile with backend="inductor" and mode="max-autotune") and Torch-TensorRT (using torch.compile with backend="torch_tensorrt" and dynamic=False). Correctness was verified by element-wise comparison of the CUTLASS kernel output against the PyTorch reference.

Auto-tuning methodology. Auto-tuning is performed by the agent as Action 5 in the Pattern Realization stage (Section 4.2). The agent infers the search space from the CUTLASS test files for the target architecture and data type, extracting valid threadblock and warp tile shapes, then sweeps pipeline stages or kernel schedules depending on the architecture. For the square matrix multiplication (Problem 1), the agent swept 14 threadblock tile shapes—7 with Ktile=16K_{\text{tile}}=16 and 7 with Ktile=32K_{\text{tile}}=32, spanning instruction shapes 16×16×1616\times 16\times 16 and 16×16×3216\times 16\times 32—crossed with 7 pipeline stages (2–8), yielding 98 configurations in total. Each configuration was compiled as a standalone shared library, executed with 5 warmup iterations followed by 20 timed iterations, and measured using time.perf_counter with CUDA synchronization. All reported timings are averaged over 20 trials; variance was negligible (<1% across configurations), so we report means only. Performance is reported in TFLOPS and as a percentage of the relevant peak throughput (156 TFLOPS for TF32, 312 TFLOPS for FP16 on A100). Configurations that exceeded shared-memory capacity or register limits at high pipeline stages were recorded as launch failures (status 7).

5.2. Evaluation Results

For each KernelBench problem, we report the output of all three stages of the workflow. Stage 1 (Pattern Discovery) describes the patterns the agent identified from the computation graph. Stage 2 (Pattern Realization) presents correctness verification, auto-tuning results, and performance comparisons against the PyTorch cuBLAS baseline. Stage 3 (Pattern Composition) applies only to multi-operator problems (Level 2 and above), where multiple realized kernels are composed into a single optimized computation graph; for single-operator Level 1 problems this stage is trivial and omitted. In this section we present results for KernelBench Problems 1, 3, and 6 (Level 1 GEMMs) and for Level 3 problem 44_MiniGPTBlock. Results for additional problems targeting the H200 GPU are in progress.

5.2.1. KernelBench Problem 1: Square Matrix Multiplication

Stage 1. The agent analyzed the computation graph of the square matrix multiplication benchmark and proposed two optimization patterns, listed in Listing 1.

Pattern p1 targets Ampere’s TF32 tensor cores with a multistage software pipeline using cp.async for data prefetching, which is the standard high-performance configuration for GEMM on SM80. Pattern p2 proposed a Hopper warp-specialized design with TMA, targeting the H200; this pattern was deferred to future evaluation on Hopper hardware. The agent prioritized p1 for immediate realization due to hardware availability.

Stage 2. The CUTLASS kernel for pattern p1 was synthesized based on CUTLASS example 41 and successfully passed correctness verification at sizes 512, 1024, and 2048 with bit-exact agreement against PyTorch’s cuBLAS output. The agent then performed auto-tuning (Action 5) by inferring the search space from the CUTLASS test files for the target architecture and data type, sweeping 98 configurations across 14 tile shapes and pipeline stages 2–8. Of these, 66 executed successfully and 32 failed due to shared-memory or register overflow at high pipeline stages.

Figure 4 (a) plots all 66 successful configurations as a scatter of hardware efficiency versus speedup over PyTorch. The majority of configurations cluster between 45–77% efficiency, with only the Ktile=32K_{\text{tile}}=32 variants reaching above 70%. The best overall configuration—threadblock tile 128×256×32128\times 256\times 32 with 3 pipeline stages (marked by the star)—achieves 124.4 TFLOPS (79.8% of peak) and a 1.14×1.14\times speedup over PyTorch. The PyTorch baseline itself sits at 70.3% of peak, confirming that cuBLAS is well-optimized for this problem size; the auto-tuned CUTLASS kernel surpasses it by finding a tile shape and stage count better matched to the A100’s memory hierarchy. By contrast, the default configuration used during initial verification (128×128×16128\times 128\times 16, 3 stages) reached only 65.0% efficiency, underscoring the importance of systematic auto-tuning.

5.2.2. KernelBench Problem 3: Batched Matrix Multiplication

Stage 1. The agent analyzed the computation graph of the batched matrix multiplication benchmark (A∈ℝ128×512×1024A\in\mathbb{R}^{128\times 512\times 1024}, B∈ℝ128×1024×2048B\in\mathbb{R}^{128\times 1024\times 2048}) and proposed a Batched GEMM pattern with TF32 tensor cores, listed in Listing 2.

The agent identified CUTLASS’s kBatched mode as the natural mapping for torch.bmm: each of the 128 independent GEMMs in the batch is dispatched to a separate tile grid, with the batch dimension providing ample parallelism to saturate all 108 SMs. TF32 was chosen as the data type to leverage tensor core throughput while maintaining close-to-FP32 accuracy.

Stage 2. The CUTLASS kernel for pattern p1 was synthesized based on CUTLASS example 05 and passed correctness verification with all 30 auto-tuned configurations achieving maximum element-wise differences below 10−310^{-3}. The agent swept 30 configurations across tile shapes and pipeline stages. Figure 4 (b) plots the results: configurations with wider N-dimension tiles (Ntile=256N_{\text{tile}}=256) consistently outperform narrower variants, and the best configuration achieves 73.3% of peak. The best configuration—threadblock tile 128×256×32128\times 256\times 32 with 3 pipeline stages—achieves 114.4 TFLOPS (73.3% of peak) and a 1.18×1.18\times speedup over PyTorch cuBLAS. The 18% improvement over the vendor library demonstrates that CUTLASS can match or exceed cuBLAS even for batched workloads, which are a common building block in attention mechanisms and recurrent networks.

5.2.3. KernelBench Problem 6: Large-K Matrix Multiplication

Stage 1. The agent analyzed the computation graph of the large-K matrix multiplication benchmark (A∈ℝ256×524,288A\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times 524{,}288}, B∈ℝ524,288×256B\in\mathbb{R}^{524{,}288\times 256}) and proposed a Stream-K GEMM pattern, listed in Listing 3.

The extreme K/M aspect ratio (2048) makes Stream-K the appropriate grid-level scheduling policy (Osama et al., 2023): with only 256 output elements per row, standard Data Parallel tiling produces too few full tiles to saturate all 108 SMs, whereas Stream-K assigns fractional K-tiles to thread blocks for even load distribution. During Stage 2 verification, the agent discovered that using FP16 for both inputs and accumulator caused overflow: summing 524,288 FP16 products (each ∼\sim0.25 for uniform [0,1)[0,1) inputs) produces values up to ∼\sim131K, well beyond FP16’s maximum representable value of 65,504. The agent resolved this by switching to mixed precision—FP16 for the A and B operands (to leverage the higher throughput of FP16 tensor cores) with FP32 accumulation and FP32 output.

Stage 2. The agent then performed auto-tuning (Action 5) by inferring the search space from the CUTLASS test files, sweeping 29 configurations across 14 tile shapes and varying pipeline stages. Figure 4 (c) plots the 23 successful configurations. Of these, 23 executed successfully and 6 failed due to invalid kernel arguments or shared-memory overflow. The best configuration (64×128×6464\times 128\times 64, 4 stages) achieves a 1.06×1.06\times speedup over PyTorch, matching cuBLAS-level performance. This parity with the vendor library confirms that the agent-synthesized CUTLASS kernel is reliable enough to serve as a building block for composition into more complex multi-operator patterns (Stage 3) without introducing performance regressions. The low absolute efficiency (24.9% of FP16 peak) is inherent to the problem shape: with M=N=256, the output matrix is too small to saturate all 108 SMs of the A100 regardless of scheduling policy. The Ktile=64K_{\text{tile}}=64 configurations consistently outperform Ktile=32K_{\text{tile}}=32 variants by 5–10 percentage points, consistent with the finding from Problem 1 that larger K-tile dimensions improve throughput.

Table 2 consolidates the performance of all three problems. Across the board, the agent-synthesized CUTLASS kernels outperform the cuBLAS baseline after auto-tuning, with speedups ranging from 1.06×1.06\times to 1.18×1.18\times. The largest gains appear for the batched workload, where the 128×256×32128\times 256\times 32 tile shape better exploits the non-square output dimensions than cuBLAS’s internal heuristics. For Problems 1 and 6, the gap between the default and auto-tuned configurations (14–34 percentage points in efficiency) underscores the value of systematic tile-shape and pipeline-stage search.

To compare compiler backends under the same harness, we additionally benchmarked PyTorch Inductor and Torch-TensorRT against eager-mode PyTorch for the same four problems. Figure 5 reports speedup vs eager across FACT, Inductor, and Torch-TensorRT. For GEMM problems, the eager baseline uses cuBLAS TF32; for MiniGPT, eager corresponds to the same PyTorch baseline module used in our other measurements.

5.2.4. KernelBench Level 3: MiniGPT Block (44_MiniGPTBlock)

We evaluate KernelBench Level 3 problem 44_MiniGPTBlock: a causal self-attention block paired with a two-layer MLP (expansion to 3072, GELU, projection to 768), at (B,T,C)=(128,512,768)(B,T,C)=(128,512,768) on the same A100 hardware and PyTorch eager baseline as above.

Stage 1. The agent analyzed the traced computation graph and proposed multiple patterns; the two highest-priority patterns selected for realization were FMHA over the attention subgraph (pattern p1) and fused GEMM+GELU for the MLP subgraph (pattern p2), summarized in Listing 4.

Stage 2. Pattern p1 was realized as a fused multi-head attention kernel (FMHA) and verified against the PyTorch reference at multiple (B,T)(B,T) settings; the deployed configuration used queries_per_block=64, keys_per_block=128, and aligned tiling. Pattern p2 was realized as a CUTLASS GEMM with GELU epilogue fusion for the MLP; the agent auto-tuned tile and pipeline parameters (best threadblock tile 128×256×32128\times 256\times 32, warp tile 64×64×3264\times 64\times 32, 4 pipeline stages), with all reported configurations passing correctness at element-wise tolerance 10−310^{-3}.

Stage 3. The two extensions were composed into a single ModelNew module (PyTorch extensions loaded from the pattern table), replacing the attention and MLP subgraphs while preserving numerics. End-to-end benchmarks used 5 warmup and 20 timed iterations on the reference shape (128,512,768)(128,512,768). With both patterns enabled, the optimized model achieves 2.79×2.79\times speedup over the PyTorch baseline (71.5 ms →\rightarrow 25.6 ms) at 8054 GFLOPS reported by the harness (≈\approx41% of theoretical FP32 peak on A100). To isolate contributions on the full block, we additionally benchmarked configurations that load only one extension: FMHA optimized with MLP still in PyTorch yields 1.16×1.16\times speedup (71.48 ms →\rightarrow 61.68 ms), while MLP+GELU optimized with attention still in PyTorch yields 2.02×2.02\times (71.54 ms →\rightarrow 35.36 ms); speedups use the baseline time from the same run as each optimized measurement. Figure 6 plots these end-to-end latencies and speedups.

5.3. Discussion

Key findings. Our evaluation demonstrates that library-grounded agentic kernel synthesis can achieve competitive performance on both single-operator and multi-pattern workloads. On Level-1 GEMM problems, auto-tuned CUTLASS kernels achieved 1.06×\times–1.18×\times speedups over PyTorch’s cuBLAS baseline, with the strongest improvement (1.18×\times) on batched GEMM where cuBLAS’s heuristics are less tuned for irregular shapes. On Level-3, the MiniGPT block achieved 2.79×\times end-to-end speedup through multi-pattern composition, demonstrating that the workflow’s value increases with pattern complexity. Per-pattern ablations revealed that MLP+GELU fusion contributed most of the speedup (2.02×\times alone), while FMHA provided marginal benefit (1.16×\times)—suggesting that the choice of which patterns to optimize depends on workload characteristics.

Compiler baseline comparison. We additionally evaluated PyTorch Inductor and Torch-TensorRT on the same four problems. For GEMM problems (Problems 1, 3, and 6), both compiler backends produced kernels slower than eager PyTorch (0.86×\times–0.88×\times), likely due to compilation overhead and suboptimal kernel selection for these specific problem sizes. For the MiniGPT block, Inductor achieved 1.86×\times and Torch-TensorRT achieved 1.81×\times speedups—both substantially lower than FACT’s 2.79×\times, indicating that multi-pattern composition with library-grounded kernels outperforms general-purpose compiler optimization for this workload. These results suggest that agentic CUTLASS synthesis complements rather than replaces compiler backends: it excels when workload-specific patterns are known, while compilers provide broader coverage.

6. Related Work

Agentic GPU kernel generation and optimization. Recent work demonstrates that LLM-driven agents can generate and optimize CUDA kernels by closing the loop with compilation, correctness checking, and profiling. KernelBlaster proposes memory-augmented in-context RL to transfer optimization knowledge across tasks and improve KernelBench speedups (Dong et al., 2026). CUDA Agent scales agentic RL with automated verification/profiling to learn high-performance CUDA kernel generation behavior (Dai et al., 2026). StitchCUDA extends this direction to end-to-end GPU programs with a planner/coder/verifier decomposition and rubric-based RL, emphasizing robust rewards from real executions (Li et al., 2026). Astra studies a multi-agent workflow that starts from existing CUDA kernels (rather than purely from high-level specs) and iteratively applies profiling-driven transformations to improve performance (Wei et al., 2025).

LLM-guided optimization for accelerators and compilers. Autocomp targets tensor accelerators and frames optimization as an LLM-driven search guided by domain knowledge and hardware feedback, and shows that optimization schedules can be reused across related tensor operations (Hong et al., 2025).

Subgraph-aware auto-tuning. Closest to our dynamic pattern table is prior work on exploiting subgraph similarities for efficient auto-tuning (Li et al., 2023), which introduces FamilySeer, a framework that caches and reuses tuning results across similar tensor program subgraphs. Our work differs in three key respects: (1) we use LLM agents to discover patterns automatically rather than relying on manual subgraph extraction; (2) our pattern table is indexed by architecture, data type, and shape in addition to subgraph structure; and (3) we focus on CUTLASS template instantiation rather than search-space exploration within a single compiler backend.

Library-centric execution engines and tuning. CUrator focuses on efficient LLM execution by integrating CUDA libraries (cuBLAS/CUTLASS) through compiler infrastructure and profiling-driven selection of tiling and split-K strategies for GEMM variants (Lee et al., 2025). Collectively, these systems motivate our focus on expanding the search space to newer CUTLASS 3.x kernel schedules (e.g., warp-specialized cooperative and pingpong) and enabling agent-driven exploration for Hopper-specific performance regimes.

7. Conclusion and Future Work

We presented FACT, a framework that combines library-grounded agentic kernel synthesis with a dynamic pattern registry and architecture-specific auto-tuning. Our three-stage workflow—Pattern Discovery, Pattern Realization, and Pattern Composition—enables LLM agents to optimize PyTorch modules by instantiating CUTLASS templates for multi-operator patterns, with mandatory auto-tuning that infers search spaces from CUTLASS test files. On KernelBench Level-1 GEMM problems, auto-tuned CUTLASS kernels achieved 1.06×\times–1.18×\times speedups over PyTorch’s cuBLAS baseline. On a Level-3 MiniGPT block, composing fused multi-head attention with fused MLP GEMM+GELU yielded 2.79×\times end-to-end speedup, outperforming compiler baselines (Inductor: 1.86×\times, Torch-TensorRT: 1.81×\times).

Future work. Several directions remain for extending FACT. First, we are extending the framework to support Hopper architecture (H200 GPU), targeting warp-specialized kernels with TMA and WGMMA instructions. Second, we plan to compare FACT against agentic baselines (KernelBlaster, CUDA Agent, StitchCUDA, Astra) on the same KernelBench problems to quantify the benefits of library-grounded synthesis. Finally, we are working on open-sourcing the generated CUTLASS kernels and workflow prototype to enable reproducibility and community engagement.
